content:
The right assistive devices can transform daily life with arthritis, making tasks easier and reducing joint strain. Many items are available free through the NHS or your local council, while others can be purchased affordably from UK retailers.

Quick answer: Assistive devices can help manage arthritis by making daily tasks easier and reducing joint strain. Examples include kitchen aids like electric tin openers, kettle tippers, and ergonomic utensils. For the bathroom, grab rails, shower seats, and raised toilet seats are available. Dressing aids such as long-handled shoe horns and sock aids can assist, while mobility aids like walking sticks and wheelchairs can improve movement.

Kitchen Aids

  • Electric tin opener — eliminates hand twisting (from £10)
  • Jar opener (under-cabinet) — grips the lid so you only need to turn the jar (from £5)
  • Kettle tipper — cradle for your kettle that pours without lifting (from £15)
  • Ergonomic utensils — thick, soft-grip handles for knives, peelers, and spoons (from £8)
  • One-handed chopping board — with spikes and corner grip to hold food steady (from £20)
  • Perching stool — sit while working at kitchen counters (from £30, or free via OT)

Bathroom Aids

  • Grab rails — for bath, shower, and toilet (from £10, often fitted free by council)
  • Shower seat/stool — sit safely while showering (from £20, or free via OT)
  • Raised toilet seat — reduces the distance you need to bend (from £15)
  • Long-handled sponge — reach your back and feet without bending (from £5)
  • Lever taps — easier to turn than round taps (tap turners from £3)

Dressing Aids

  • Long-handled shoe horn — put on shoes without bending (from £3)
  • Button hook — fasten buttons one-handed (from £5)
  • Elastic shoelaces — turn lace-ups into slip-ons (from £4)
  • Sock aid — put on socks without bending down (from £5)
  • Zip puller — large loop to grip zip pulls easily (from £3)

Mobility Aids

  • Walking stick — reduces load on hip and knee by up to 25% (from £10)
  • Walking frame/rollator — four-wheeled with seat for resting (from £50)
  • Ergonomic crutches — forearm crutches with soft grips (from £30)
  • Wheelchair — for longer distances; available through NHS wheelchair services

Where to Get Free Equipment

  • NHS occupational therapy — ask your GP for an OT referral for home assessment and free equipment
  • Local council — contact adult social care for a community OT assessment
  • Disabled Facilities Grant — up to £30,000 (England) for major home adaptations like stairlifts and wet rooms
  • British Red Cross — short-term loan of wheelchairs and mobility aids

Where to Buy in the UK

  • Ability Superstore — comprehensive online shop for disability aids
  • NRS Healthcare — wide range with next-day delivery
  • Amazon UK — search "arthritis aids" for extensive range
  • Argos — mobility aids and bathroom equipment
  • Local mobility shops — try equipment before buying

Don't struggle in silence — simple aids can make a huge difference. Start with a free OT assessment to find out what's available to you.

Practical next steps for Assistive Devices for Arthritis – UK Buyer's Guide

If you came here about Assistive Devices for Arthritis – UK Buyer's Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Quick questions about Assistive Devices Arthritis Buyer

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
